Brics backs Gaza ceasefire, calls for two-state solution for Palestine

Brics leaders on Saturday adopted a joint declaration calling for the extension of the “ceasefire” in Gaza and backing a two-state solution for Palestine. 

The declaration said root causes of conflicts must be tackled and reiterated the group's commitment to peaceful resolution through “dialogue, consultation and diplomacy”. 

The group, which comprises Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates, also raised concerns over the increasing nuclear risks and emphasised that nuclear safeguards, safety and security must be upheld, including in armed conflicts.

items.title: Iran praises Houthi victory along strategic Red Sea coast as ‘divine triumph’
items.summary_raw:
Iran praises Houthi victory along strategic Red Sea coast as ‘divine triumph’

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has congratulated Yemen’s Houthis following reports of them seizing the entire Red Sea coastline of the country.

The advance was described by IRGC spokesman Sardar Mohebi as a “divine triumph” and the culmination of years of resistance by the group.

The Houthis’ advance represents a “divine triumph and the fruit of years of steadfastness in the most difficult of battlefields”, Mohebi wrote on X.

Iranian officials have continued to hail the Houthi gains.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said that “the homegrown resolve of the resistance have driven the US and its allies into a tactical and strategic impasse”.

Nearly 500 refugees, including women and children, from Yemen have arrived in Djibouti’s coastal city of Obock, according to the country’s minister of economy and finance, Ilyas Dawaleh.

Dawaleh wrote on X that the refugees were rescued at sea from boats stranded without fuel. 

At least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, the UN’s International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday.

Yemeni government-run Executive Unit for the Management of Displaced Persons Camps said 1,367 families were displaced on 8 September alone in the provinces of Taiz, Al-Hudaydah and Lahj.

Iranian media: Houthis take control of Strait of Mandeb after seizing Mayyun Island

Yemen’s Houthis control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait after seizing Mayyun Island, also known as Perim Island, Iran’s Tasnim News Agency reported.

Located at the centre of the Bab al-Mandab Strait,  Mayyun Island is a key monitoring point overlooking the vital maritime passage.

Two Yemeni sources also told Reuters that Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had withdrawn from Perim Island.

The development came after Houthis seized the western coastal city of Mocha, forcing the government forces to retreat toward the south and the city of Dhubab.

The Sanaa-based Yemen Press Agency, citing field sources, said Houthi forces seized the al-Omari camp overlooking the strait.

items.title: Türkiye's Foreign Ministry released archival photographs and Ottoman-script documents from its own collections, showing what it says are massacres of Turkish civilians and burned v…
items.summary_raw: Türkiye's Foreign Ministry released archival photographs and Ottoman-script documents from its own collections, showing what it says are massacres of Turkish civilians and burned villages by the Greek army during the 1919–1922 occupation of western Anatolia.   The images focus on villages near Bursa — including Mashara Hasan (100 of 110 buildings burned, bodies of civilians photographed by an inquiry commission) and Söğütpınar (residents forced into a mosque, killed by bayonets and gunfire).  The ministry cited Article 59 of the Treaty of Lausanne, where Greece formally recognized its obligation to pay reparations for acts "contrary to the laws of war" in Anatolia — though Türkiye waived those claims given Greece's financial condition.

items.title: Satellite images show smoke near Saudi Arabia’s critical East-West oil pipeline
items.summary_raw:
Satellite images show smoke near Saudi Arabia’s critical East-West oil pipeline

Satellite images showed smoke rising near Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, one of the kingdom’s key energy assets, Reuters has reported.

The news agency said Saudi authorities did not immediately report any incident at the site.

The East-West Pipeline has become increasingly important for Saudi Arabia during the Iran war, enabling state oil giant Aramco to ship crude from the kingdom’s eastern coast to the Red Sea on its western coast.

It offers an alternative route for sending crude through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic global energy chokepoint.

In a separate, nearly four-hour pre-election interview, Siegmund described “remigration” primarily as reversing what he calls misguided migration, including deporting people legally required to leave Germany.

Iran dismisses IAEA resolution, says nonproliferation accusations political

Iran has dismissed a resolution passed by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which accuses Tehran of failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation commitments and refers the matter to the UN Security Council.

“Renewed accusations against Iran’s peaceful nuclear program are political and not technical in nature,” Iran's UN ambassador, Gholamhossein Darzi, said in a letter addressed to the Security Council president, IRNA reported.

“The Islamic Republic of Iran categorically rejects the baseless accusations and distortions raised by some members in this meeting regarding Iran’s peaceful nuclear program,” Darzi said.

items.summary_raw: ELINT News RT @EGYOSINT: 🇸🇦🇾🇪 The Houthis appear to have struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, which carries crude from Abqaiq on the Gulf coast to Yanbu on the Red Sea.  Multiple fire hotspots were detected at six points along the pipeline route at roughly the same time, around 17:56 UTC.   Large smoke plumes were also visible in the attached NOAA-20 and MODIS satellite imagery.  Looks like the Houthis might have actually scored a direct hit on the E/W pipeline. Confidence flag is tagged at maximum, and FRP printing above 70 MW blows way past conventional fire(~30 MW).  FRP >70 MW scream high-pressure crude rupture and blowout conflagration. Brightness is literally maxing out and clipping the saturation cap on the VIIRS I4 band.  Cross-referencing the delta between VIIRS and MODIS orbital passes, FRP anomaly printed 60+ MW for an 8 hour duration minimum. A garden-variety valve leak or routine gas venting simply cannot sustain that burn duration or heat signature.  Faded the controlled burn or flare stack hypothesis too. Pump stations sit dozens of clicks apart on the ROW, but these heat anomalies are tightly clustered along a sub-10km stretch.  No normal maintenance operation

items.summary_raw: Vice President JD Vance privately sought direct, unfiltered assessments from U.S. military commanders about the Iran war, and what he heard was much more concerning than the administration’s public message.   Commanders warned that the war was draining critical U.S. weapons stockpiles, particularly Patriot interceptors and long-range missiles, while potentially weakening America’s ability to deter China, Russia and North Korea.  They also told Vance that Iran was proving more resilient than expected and willing to absorb enormous damage rather than collapse.  Vance, who had opposed the war before it began, used these private assessments to advise Trump and became increasingly involved in efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict.  Source: NYT

Emissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper says

Rising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are transforming the world’s forests, wetlands and tundra to the point they are releasing emissions that could further worsen global heating by as much as 30%, a new study has found.

As the world heats up, permafrost in the high latitudes is thawing, fiercer wildfires are burning in drying forests and wetlands and lakes are warming. All of these changes are themselves causing the release of planet-heating methane and carbon dioxide locked in trees and soils, therefore worsening the climate crisis, the paper states.

items.title: How the fate of a small furry animal reveals the ecological tragedy of Israel’s war on Lebanon | Hisham Younes
items.summary_raw:
The Syrian rock hyrax depends on the fragile landscapes of the border region. Alongside other environmentalists, I have been documenting the destruction of its habitat

Wars are usually measured in the number of people killed, homes destroyed and towns erased. Far less attention is paid to what happens beneath the rubble. Across southern Lebanon, repeated large-scale detonations are not only causing human tragedy by demolishing villages, they are also destroying the ancient limestone habitats that have sheltered colonies of rock hyrax for centuries.

As founder and president of Green Southerners, an environmental organisation documenting the ecological effects of war in southern Lebanon, I have been helping colleagues to record the damage inflicted on forests, wildlife and fragile ecosystems across the border region.

items.title: Is Burnham trying to appease Trump? Or Reform? What other reason is there for these North Sea oil plans? | George Monbiot
items.summary_raw:
Climate catastrophe is on our doorstep – yet Labour’s impending approval of further drilling will bring more pain for negligible gains

Pinch yourself, it’s happening again. Here is a Labour government spending a vast amount of political capital to earn tiny material gains while risking huge political losses. It occurred repeatedly under Keir Starmer, and now – with the impending decision to approve further gas and oil drilling in the North Sea – it is happening under Andy Burnham. You rack your brains to explain it, but no rational explanation comes.

Burnham is studiously cryptic about his reasons. His clearest statement to date goes as follows: “There is a resource there. When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that.” Does he mean that oil and gas workers are struggling? If so, this decision will be of little use to them. items.title: The Tyranny of Shipyard Cost-Plus Contracting

items.title: Reclaiming the streets: the architects clawing back Europe’s car-centric spaces
items.summary_raw:
The European Prize for Urban Public Space’s shortlist highlights projects helping people cope with climate crisis

In the words of Joni Mitchell, the planners of many urban centres around the world “paved paradise and put up a parking lot”. The European Prize for Urban Public Space tries to show that cities don’t have to be locked in the automotive age for ever.

The prize’s latest shortlist, announced on Wednesday, highlights architectural projects that convert infrastructure for cars into spaces that help urban dwellers cope with the soaring temperatures of the climate crisis: roundabouts that have become splash pools, thoroughfares turned into green havens, and car parks into gardens.

Several ballistic missile and cluster submunition impacts were recorded, despite the U.S. launching close to 100 Patriot PAC-2/3 interceptors.   As usual, the U.S. has not struck any of the Iranian ballistic missile launchers after the attacks, and have subsequently significantly decreased their already-depleted interceptor missile stockpiles.  In the coming hours, Iran may attack U.S. bases in Bahrain, Qatar, and Kuwait, along with oil tankers docked near Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, with drones and/or missiles, as the IRGC Navy warned earlier.

items.title: The world is adapting to extreme heat — but not nearly fast enough
A key limitation of Greece’s €3 billion Achilles’ Shield agreement with Israel is that Greece will not receive the source code for the command-and-control (C2) systems.  Moshe Pate…
items.summary_raw: A key limitation of Greece’s €3 billion Achilles’ Shield agreement with Israel is that Greece will not receive the source code for the command-and-control (C2) systems.  Moshe Patel, head of Israel’s Missile Defense Organization, said source-code access was not included in the licensing agreement, despite Athens’ interest in maintaining control over the software architecture of the new air-defense network.  Israel will instead provide ongoing support, maintenance and future technical assistance.   This means Greece will operate the Spyder, Barak MX and David’s Sling systems without full access to the underlying proprietary software controlling them.  Source: Kathimerini

This pressure campaign by the People’s Republic of China began intensifying in 2022. items.title: Nepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster
items.summary_raw:
Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions

Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.

Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.

items.title: Global move away from oil could lead to conflict and migration, experts say
items.summary_raw:
Researchers urge governments to help worst afflicted countries, such as Nigeria and Algeria, which rely on oil revenues for public services

Conflict, migration and economic upheaval will accompany the global move away from oil, unless governments act urgently to help the worst afflicted countries to cope, research has found.

Nigeria, Iran, Angola and Algeria are among the countries that will be severely affected, as they rely strongly on oil revenues for their government and provision of public services, but have little diversification and too little capital to cushion the blow.

items.title: Pakistan Air Force officially revealed Türkiye's KORKUT 35mm anti-aircraft gun system in its Defence Day video, the first confirmation of induction.   The PAF showed a layered air …
items.summary_raw: Pakistan Air Force officially revealed Türkiye's KORKUT 35mm anti-aircraft gun system in its Defence Day video, the first confirmation of induction.   The PAF showed a layered air defense stack.  Chinese HQ-17 SAMs, Turkish KORKUT guns (twin 35mm, 1,100 rounds per minute, 4km range with airburst ammo), and Turkish ŞAHİN 40mm counter-drone turrets.   The same video featured multiple Turkish drones including AKINCI and Bayraktar TB2.   The combination is designed as a gun-missile-point defense layer against drones, loitering munitions, and low-flying aircraft.

The two co-founders, George Gemelas and George Behrakis outlined the project in an op-ed published in this newspaper two weeks ago that is well worth reading. More information is available on the organization’s webpage. We are in fact living through a moment in which the diaspora, including Greek-Americans, can help their homeland which is facing a crisis.

items.title: Air conditioners are our best bet in the fight against extreme heat – whether we like it or not
items.summary_raw:
Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis

The greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to “degrow” the economy and to curb the population. The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.

Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation over air conditioning.

items.title: Three-Day Mourning for Armed Forces – Who Were the Two Phantom Pilots and What Investigators Are Examining
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS. One day after the tragedy at Tanagra, the Hellenic Air Force is in deep mourning, while the investigation into the crash of the F-4E Phantom II has moved to the center of attention. The two pilots who lost their lives were Air Force officers Ioannis Blesias, 40, and Dimitrios Petrou, 37, both experienced aviators. The aircraft belonged to the 338 Squadron “Aris” of the 117 Combat Wing. The two pilots had more than 1,500 flight hours, according to information available so far. Defense Minister Nikos Dendias declared three days of mourning across the Armed Forces, from Saturday, September 5, through Monday, September 7, following the deaths of the two crew members. The special committee investigating the crash is now examining every available piece of evidence from the fatal flight. The material collected includes videos from the air show, television footage and videos recorded by members of the public, while recorded communications with the control tower are expected to be particularly important.
